issues.subcategory: Dummy/randomized data presented as findings
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly states that the methods and results were written using a randomized Qualtrics-generated dataset and will be updated after data collection. This means the reported participant characteristics, inferential statistics, p-values, effect sizes, and conclusions are not empirical findings. Presenting simulated/random data in an abstract and results section as if it supports or fails to support hypotheses makes the manuscript impossible to evaluate as a completed empirical study and risks misleading readers.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: Dummy/randomized data in methods/results
issues.description: The paper explicitly indicates that the methods and results sections are placeholders based on randomized data rather than actual collected observations. Consequently, all reported inferential results, descriptive statistics, participant exclusions, and interpretations lack evidentiary value.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory data-collection status
issues.description: The manuscript says data collection had already been launched or completed before analysis, but elsewhere says the reported results are from randomized dummy data and will be updated after actual data collection. These statements are mutually inconsistent and obscure whether any real data exist, whether analyses were conducted after data collection, and whether the study is prospective or retrospective.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period... All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.subcategory: Nonrandom assignment/self-selection into conditions
issues.description: The procedure states that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. This destroys random assignment, permits systematic self-selection into conditions, and invalidates causal comparisons among intervention and victim-identifiability conditions. The original design depended on random assignment; self-selection creates confounding by participant preferences, charitable orientation, prior attitudes, comprehension, and other traits.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction about experimental design
issues.description: The design is described as within-subject, but the tables and analyses treat identifiability and intervention as between-subject factors, with separate sample sizes per condition summing to N = 1000. A true within-subject design would require each participant to experience multiple conditions and would need repeated-measures or mixed-model analyses. This inconsistency affects the appropriateness of the analysis and interpretation.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.subcategory: Wrong analysis for stated within-subject design
issues.description: If the study is truly within-subject, a standard independent-groups 2 x 3 ANOVA with residual df = 994 is inappropriate because it ignores dependency among repeated observations. A repeated-measures ANOVA or multilevel model would be required. If the analysis is correct for a between-subject design, then the design description is wrong.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: Combining distinct original studies changes manipulation structure
issues.description: The replication merges Studies 1 and 3 into one experiment and applies the explicit intervention to the joint condition, which was not part of the original Study 3. This materially changes the design and introduces new combinations of manipulations. It is therefore not a close replication of either original study and may alter psychological processes through contrast, demand characteristics, and carryover across conceptual manipulations.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.subcategory: Imaginary donation replaces real monetary behavior
issues.description: The original dependent variable involved donating real money participants had received. The replication uses hypothetical/imaginary donation from $0 to $5. Hypothetical donation intentions may not validly capture actual charitable giving and are vulnerable to social desirability, scale-use artifacts, and lack of incentive compatibility. This is a major construct-validity deviation for the primary outcome.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Removal of earned-money endowment
issues.description: The original participants received five one-dollar bills from a prior survey and then could donate them. The replication removes the endowment and prior task. Endowment source, payment salience, and physical possession of cash are known to influence giving, so this change may alter the donation process substantially.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: Online MTurk sample differs from original lab/student-center sample
issues.description: The study uses MTurk/online participants rather than people in a university student center/laboratory context. This changes participant population, attention environment, payment context, and potential experience with psychology studies. The manuscript labels the study close to very close but does not adequately address how these differences limit comparability and generalizability.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: Sampling source inconsistent or unspecified
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between Qualtrics-generated responses, MTurk workers, and unspecified geographic origin/compensation. This makes the actual recruitment frame unclear and impairs evaluation of sample quality, eligibility, and generalizability.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration... Geographic origin | US American | Not specified... MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.subcategory: Missing recruitment and compensation details
issues.description: The methods do not report essential details such as recruitment platform details, inclusion criteria, country restrictions, compensation amount, approval procedures, data-quality screening rules, or how participants were prevented from repeat participation. These omissions prevent assessment of sample validity and replication fidelity.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: Exclusion based on prior knowledge without details
issues.description: Participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those failing attention checks were excluded, but the manuscript does not report how prior knowledge was assessed, what the attention check was, whether exclusions were preregistered, how many were excluded, or whether exclusions differed by condition. Such exclusions can bias results, especially if assessed post-treatment.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: No accounting of exclusions or missing data
issues.description: The manuscript provides no participant flow, number recruited, number excluded for prior knowledge, attention failures, incomplete responses, or missing data by condition. Without these details, the final N and condition balance cannot be evaluated, and attrition or exclusion bias remains unaddressed.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc t-test signs inconsistent with means
issues.description: In Table 10, the identifiable versus statistical comparison reports t = -2.40 but d = 0.076 and is interpreted as statistical victims donating more. A positive d conflicts with the negative t if the contrast is identifiable minus statistical. The direction and coding of effect sizes are unclear and likely incorrect.

issues.subcategory: Descriptive means contradict reported interpretation
issues.description: The interpretation says statistical-victim participants donated more than identifiable-victim participants with means M = 2.54 and M = 2.24. However, the cell means in Table 7 imply identifiable overall mean around 2.54 and statistical overall mean around 2.25, the reverse. This suggests a labeling, computation, or reporting error in the post-hoc results.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: Condition means do not match marginal means
issues.description: Table 7 gives identifiable condition means of 2.58 and 2.50 and statistical condition means of 2.46 and 2.01. Weighted over the reported sample sizes, the identifiable marginal mean should be approximately 2.54 and the statistical marginal mean approximately 2.25, not the reverse stated in the text. This undermines confidence in the analyses and conclusions.

issues.subcategory: Confidence interval incompatible with reported significant post-hoc test
issues.description: The identifiable-versus-statistical post-hoc comparison is marked significant with pBonferroni = .049, but the reported 95% CI for d is [-0.05, 0.20], which includes zero. Although adjusted p-values and unadjusted CIs can sometimes differ if not aligned, this is not explained and suggests inconsistent reporting or mismatched intervals.

issues.subcategory: Implausible effect-size confidence intervals
issues.description: Several reported partial eta-squared confidence intervals have lower bounds of exactly 0.00 and very narrow ranges, including for significant effects. It is unclear how these CIs were computed, whether they are for partial eta-squared, and whether they are one-sided or truncated. Lack of method details and possible truncation reduce interpretability.

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate contrast after changing design
issues.description: The contrast compares the identifiable/no-intervention condition against the average of five other conditions. This differs from the original contrast against three other cells and combines conceptually different conditions, including the joint condition and explicit intervention applied to joint stimuli. The contrast no longer tests the original hypothesis cleanly and may dilute or distort effects.
issues.quote: contrast the mean difference of identifiable/no intervention on donation with the combination of 5 conditions (statistical/no intervention, statistical/intervention, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.subcategory: Original contrast t sign inconsistent with means
issues.description: In Table 11, the original identifiable/no-intervention mean is 2.83 and other-conditions mean is 1.26, yet the t statistic is reported as -4.06. If the contrast is identifiable/no-intervention minus other conditions, the sign should be positive. This indicates unclear coding or a sign error.
issues.quote: Identifiable/ no intervention | 2.83 | 2.10 | 117 | -4.06... Other conditions | 1.26 | 1.74 | 117 | -4.06

issues.subcategory: df and sample size inconsistencies in original-study reporting
issues.description: For Study 1, N = 121 is reported, but the ANOVA uses df2 = 115, which implies six model parameters/cells or exclusions, not the expected residual df for a 2 x 2 between-subject ANOVA with N = 121. The manuscript does not explain missing observations or degrees-of-freedom differences, limiting verification of effect-size calculations.
issues.quote: Effect of identifiability and intervention on donation (Study 1) (N=121)... df1 | df2 | F... 1 | 115

issues.subcategory: Study 3 ANOVA df reporting incomplete
issues.description: Table 2 reports Study 3 with df1 = 2 but df2 = N/A despite N = 159. For a one-way ANOVA with three groups, the residual df should be available unless data are missing or analysis differed. Omitting df2 prevents independent verification of p-values and effect sizes.
issues.quote: Effect of identifiability on donation (Study 3) (N=159)... df1 | df2 | F... 2 | N/A | 5.67

issues.subcategory: Questionable conversion of interaction to Cohen's d
issues.description: The manuscript reports an interaction effect as d = 0.41 without explaining how d was derived from a factorial ANOVA interaction. Standardized mean differences for interactions require specifying a contrast and denominator; otherwise they are not directly comparable to simple main-effect d values. This affects the power analysis and replication evaluation.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis insufficiently reported
issues.description: The sample-size justification refers readers to supplementary materials but provides no alpha level, target power, assumed effect size for the primary hypothesis, allocation ratio, planned exclusions, or whether the interaction or main effect drove the sample size. Since subgroup/cell sizes determine power in factorial designs, the manuscript lacks enough information to judge adequacy.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: Unequal and unexplained cell sizes
issues.description: The six cell sizes vary from 159 to 175. In a randomized factorial design this could occur by chance or quota allocation, but the manuscript gives no randomization or allocation procedure. Combined with the statement that participants selected conditions, unequal cell sizes raise concern about selection bias and unbalanced confounds.

issues.subcategory: Causal claims despite self-selection and hypothetical outcome
issues.description: The manuscript uses causal language about effects of identifiability and intervention, but the stated procedure lets participants select conditions and the outcome is hypothetical. Without random assignment and with possible confounds, causal interpretations of intervention effects are not justified.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: Correlation interpreted as prediction
issues.description: The correlation analysis is described as examining whether affective feelings predict donation. Cross-sectional correlations between feelings and donation measured in the same survey do not establish prediction or directionality and may be confounded or reflect common-method variance.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: Manipulation of deliberative thinking confounded with demand characteristics
issues.description: Explicitly teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect may alter donations through demand awareness, experimenter-demand effects, reactance, moral self-presentation, or suspicion rather than deliberative/analytical thinking per se. The manuscript treats this as a clean deliberative-thinking manipulation without reporting manipulation checks or addressing alternative mechanisms.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.subcategory: Implicit learning terminology inappropriate
issues.description: The manuscript labels the joint presentation of identifiable and statistical victims as 'implicitly learning' the identifiable victim effect. Presenting both types of information may induce comparison or alter perceived need, but it does not necessarily constitute learning about the effect. The terminology conflates implicit deliberation, joint evaluation, and learning.
issues.quote: Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim

issues.subcategory: Aggregated feelings composite insufficiently justified
issues.description: The manuscript aggregates heterogeneous constructs—upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and sometimes perceived impact—without reporting scale items, response anchors, factor structure, internal consistency, or theoretical justification. Combining affective, moral, cognitive, and efficacy judgments may obscure construct-specific effects and weaken validity.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: Perceived impact treated inconsistently as affective feeling
issues.description: Perceived impact of donation is conceptually an efficacy or outcome-expectancy judgment, not an affective feeling. The manuscript includes it among 'segregated affective reactions' and sometimes as an extension, creating construct confusion and potentially contaminating the aggregated feelings measure if included.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 6 contradicts abstract result
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts that identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims, but the abstract states that perceived impact is lower for identifiable or joint identifiable-statistical victims. This inconsistency indicates either a reversed prediction, misinterpreted result, or reporting error.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: Abstract result contradicts hypothesis and reported post-hoc result
issues.description: The abstract claims people have lower perceived impact ratings when facing an identifiable victim or identifiable victim with statistics. In the results, the only significant post-hoc comparison is statistical versus joint, and no significant identifiable-versus-statistical difference is reported. The abstract overstates and mischaracterizes the result.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Multiple testing without adequate control
issues.description: The manuscript conducts numerous ANOVAs and post-hoc tests across donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, interactions, and correlations. Although Bonferroni is used for some pairwise tests, there is no family-wise or false-discovery control across the many dependent variables and hypotheses, increasing Type I error risk, especially for the extension finding p = .045.
issues.quote: We conducted a  2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.subcategory: Conditional post-hoc testing rules unclear and flexible
issues.description: The analysis plan states that some post-hoc tests are conducted only if effects are significant, but the criteria differ by table and include main effects, intervention, and interaction. Conditional analysis decisions can inflate flexibility unless fully preregistered with exact comparisons and correction procedures.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: Pre-registration details not sufficiently reported in manuscript
issues.description: Although links are provided, the manuscript does not summarize key preregistered elements: primary outcome, primary test, exclusion rules, stopping rule, planned sample size after exclusions, manipulation checks, and deviations. Readers should not need external files to determine whether the reported analyses were confirmatory.
issues.quote: Pre-registration on the Open Science Framework | <https://osf.io/n4jkh/?view_only=d52771c7540a4a8f8051c8b430a6f15d>

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous confirmatory versus exploratory status of extension
issues.description: The extension involving perceived impact is described as a hypothesis, included in segregated feelings analyses, and interpreted as supported, but it is not clear whether this was preregistered as confirmatory or exploratory, nor how it was corrected for multiple comparisons. This affects evidential strength.
issues.quote: To extend the replication, we added the “perceived impact of donation” as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: No manipulation checks reported
issues.description: The study aims to manipulate deliberative thinking explicitly and implicitly but reports no manipulation check for whether participants read, understood, or engaged in deliberative/analytical thinking. Without manipulation checks, null intervention findings are difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.subcategory: No attention to blinding or demand awareness
issues.description: The explicit intervention teaches participants the bias under study and then asks for donation decisions, creating strong demand-characteristic risks. The manuscript does not report blinding of participants to hypotheses, suspicion probes, or procedures to reduce demand effects.
issues.quote: one group learning about the identifiable victim effect from previous research while another served as a control group

issues.subcategory: Updated victim stimuli may alter effect
issues.description: The replication uses updated victim information instead of the original stimuli. Changes in victim identity, narrative vividness, severity, nationality, imagery, and charity context could affect sympathy and perceived efficacy. The manuscript labels stimuli as similar but does not document equivalence or pretest materials.
issues.quote: Updated victim information We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: Stimuli and item wording not included in manuscript
issues.description: Critical materials such as charity appeals, intervention text, victim descriptions/statistics, feeling items, scale anchors, and attention checks are not reported in the manuscript. Reliance on external links reduces transparency and makes peer review and replication difficult if links break.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.subcategory: No ethical approval or consent information
issues.description: The manuscript involves human participants and charitable-donation scenarios but does not report ethics approval, informed consent, debriefing, deception/demand management, or data privacy protections. These are necessary for evaluating research compliance and participant protection.
issues.quote: Participants

issues.subcategory: Implausible age distribution for MTurk/online sample
issues.description: The reported generated sample has mean age 67.8, SD 30.10, and age range 18–120, which is implausible for typical MTurk recruitment and likely reflects random dummy generation rather than real sampling. If real, it would require careful explanation and age-related analyses; if dummy, it should not be reported as participants.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10... Age range (years) | 18-120

issues.subcategory: Table formatting duplicates replication columns
issues.description: Table 4 contains duplicated columns or entries for the replication/Qualtrics-generated response, suggesting editing or formatting errors. Such errors make it unclear which sample characteristics apply.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: No demographic covariate or balance reporting
issues.description: The manuscript reports only age and gender, with geographic origin unspecified. It does not report condition-level demographic balance, education, income, nationality, political orientation, religiosity, prior charity behavior, or other variables that may influence donation, especially important if assignment was self-selected.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: Ordinal/count donation outcome treated as continuous without justification
issues.description: Donation is bounded from $0 to $5, likely discrete or ordinal in dollar increments. The original used ordered probit in addition to ANOVA, but the replication omits ordered probit and provides no justification or robustness checks for treating bounded donation as normally distributed continuous data.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: ANOVA assumptions not assessed
issues.description: The manuscript reports ANOVAs on bounded donation and Likert-type feeling variables but does not report checks for normality, homogeneity of variance, influential observations, or robustness alternatives. This matters for validity of p-values and confidence intervals, particularly with skewed donation outcomes.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI

issues.subcategory: Pearson correlations on bounded/ordinal variables without justification
issues.description: The correlation analysis uses Pearson correlations between aggregated feelings and donation, but donation is bounded/discrete and feelings are likely Likert-scale composites. Spearman or robust correlations, or regression models, may be more appropriate unless assumptions are justified.
issues.quote: Correlation between aggregated feelings and donation | Linear Pearson’s correlation

issues.subcategory: Results table numbering inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript says Tables 9 to 18 summarize statistical testing, but only Tables 9 to 15 are shown in the results. This suggests missing results or erroneous cross-referencing.
issues.quote: Table 9 to 18 summarise statistical testings for the hypotheses of this replication.

issues.subcategory: Table numbering conflict
issues.description: The manuscript refers to Table 7 as the replication classification table, but later Table 7 is descriptive statistics for donation. Duplicate/inconsistent numbering impairs readability and traceability.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication".

issues.subcategory: Overstatement of identifiable victim effect implications
issues.description: The introduction makes broad claims that the identifiable victim effect demonstrates unfair valuation of life and inefficient resource allocation. These claims go beyond what a donation experiment can establish and conflate descriptive psychological bias with normative efficiency without formal welfare analysis.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation

issues.subcategory: Misattribution of mechanisms
issues.description: The manuscript invokes availability heuristic, affect heuristic, proportion dominance, deliberative thinking, and perceived impact as explanations but does not clearly distinguish them or specify competing predictions. This conceptual overlap weakens the theoretical basis for hypotheses and interpretation of null or reversed effects.
issues.quote: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The “availability heuristic”... is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.subcategory: Incorrect/misleading statement about meta-analytic effect
issues.description: The manuscript says the overall meta-analytic mean effect size was only 0.05 but still describes the effect as crucial. It does not clarify the metric or implications of such a small effect, nor reconcile this with powering on much larger original effects. This may mislead about expected replicability and practical importance.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05, the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming close-to-very-close replication despite major deviations
issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as close to very close while acknowledging different DV stimuli, online MTurk setting, hypothetical donation, no earned cash, updated stimuli, and changed design. These are substantial deviations likely to affect the target effect. The classification overstates replication fidelity.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: No control for charity familiarity/trust or current events
issues.description: The donation target and victim information are updated and administered online years later, but the design does not report controls for familiarity with Save the Children, trust in the charity, current humanitarian events, political attitudes, or baseline donation tendencies. These factors may confound responses to victim information.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children

issues.subcategory: No details on randomization despite factorial design
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe how participants were randomized or allocated to the six conditions. Instead, it says participants selected conditions. Without a randomization mechanism, allocation concealment, and checks, experimental validity cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc p-values inconsistent with t values possible but unexplained
issues.description: For Table 10, t = -2.40 with df = 994 would yield an unadjusted two-sided p around .017; a Bonferroni adjustment for three comparisons would be about .050. The reported p = .049 is plausible but the manuscript does not specify the number of comparisons or whether CIs are adjusted accordingly, creating ambiguity.

issues.subcategory: Extension interpretation based on marginal significant result with tiny effect
issues.description: The perceived-impact main effect has ηp2 = .006 and p = .045, and only one Bonferroni post-hoc comparison is significant at p = .041 with d = .08. The manuscript treats this as supporting the hypothesis despite tiny effect size, multiple testing, simulated data, and a comparison not matching the stated identifiable-versus-statistical hypothesis.
issues.quote: only the result of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation yielded significant findings.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc perceived-impact result does not support stated extension hypothesis
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims. The reported significant post-hoc comparison is statistical versus joint, with statistical higher than joint. Identifiable versus statistical is not significant. Therefore the reported result does not support Hypothesis 6 as stated.
issues.quote: Identifiable VS Statistical | 994 | 0.91... pBonferroni 1.000... Statistical VS Joint | 994 | 2.47... pBonferroni .041*

issues.subcategory: No reliability estimates for feeling composite
issues.description: The manuscript uses an aggregated feelings measure but does not report Cronbach's alpha, omega, item-total correlations, or factor analysis. Without reliability information, correlations and ANOVAs involving the composite are difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: aggregated feelings across conditions

issues.subcategory: No model estimates or means for segregated feelings
issues.description: Table 13 reports only F values, p-values, and partial eta-squared for segregated feelings. It omits condition means and standard deviations, making it impossible to interpret the direction or substantive size of any effects, including the extension.
issues.quote: Summary of statistical tests for segregated feelings

issues.subcategory: No manipulation/stimulus comprehension checks reported
issues.description: Especially in online studies involving charity appeals and educational interventions, comprehension of victim statistics and intervention text is essential. The manuscript mentions attention checks only as exclusion criteria but reports no comprehension checks or pass rates.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Potential contamination from prior knowledge exclusion
issues.description: Excluding participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect may remove more experienced MTurk participants and produce a selected sample. If prior knowledge is assessed after the intervention or in a way that reveals the hypothesis, it can also bias responses. Timing and wording are not specified.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded

issues.subcategory: Claim of no direct replications not substantiated
issues.description: The introduction states there are no published direct replications 'to the best of our knowledge' but provides no systematic search strategy. Given the prominence of the topic and related meta-analysis, this claim requires support or should be softened.
issues.quote: To the best of our knowledge, there are no published direct replications of this study

issues.subcategory: Supplementary links incomplete placeholders
issues.description: Several important project links are placeholders rather than actual links. This undermines transparency claims and prevents verification of presentation materials and peer reviews.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: Authorship/contributor inconsistency
issues.description: The CRediT table lists So Chi Liu as contributing to preregistration and data-analysis peer review/verification, but this person is not listed as an author or fully described elsewhere. The role of this contributor and whether they meet authorship or acknowledgment criteria is unclear.
issues.quote: Role | Yik Chun Wong | Gilad Feldman | So Chi Liu... Pre-registration peer review / verification |  |  | X

issues.subcategory: No primary outcome hierarchy
issues.description: The manuscript lists many hypotheses and tests but does not clearly identify a single primary outcome and primary inferential comparison for replication success. Without a hierarchy, interpretation is vulnerable to selective emphasis among main effects, interactions, post-hoc contrasts, feelings, and correlations.
issues.quote: Table 3 Summary of hypotheses of the replication

issues.subcategory: Deviation from original ordered-probit analysis not justified
issues.description: The original reportedly used ordered probit regression, but the replication states this will not be conducted. Given the bounded donation outcome, dropping this robustness/primary original analysis is a researcher degree of freedom that can affect conclusions unless justified and preregistered.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: Mediation-like claims without mediation analysis
issues.description: The manuscript discusses perceived impact and affective feelings as mechanisms or mediators of the identifiable victim effect, but the analysis only tests mean differences and correlations. It cannot support mechanistic or mediation claims about why donations differ.
issues.quote: This highlights the importance of how the perceived impact of donation is linked with the identifiable victim effect in this replication.

issues.subcategory: Correlation analyses underpowered by condition not addressed
issues.description: Although total N is 1000, within-condition correlations use cell sizes around 159–175. The manuscript does not report power for detecting the original correlations within each condition, and null correlations may be underpowered for small-to-moderate effects.
issues.quote: correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions

issues.subcategory: Cultural/geographic origin unspecified
issues.description: Donation behavior and responses to African famine/victim appeals may vary by country, culture, income, and charity norms. The replication sample geographic origin is unspecified, limiting interpretation and generalizability.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: Outcome scale lacks detail
issues.description: The donation outcome is described as how much participants would donate from $0 to $5, but the manuscript does not say whether responses are continuous sliders, integer dollar choices, forced-choice increments, or text entry. This affects analysis choice and comparability to the original five one-dollar-bill donation measure.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5

issues.subcategory: No software/version/package details
issues.description: The manuscript says JAMOVI and R were used but does not provide software versions, packages, functions, model specifications, contrast coding, or CI computation methods. This impedes reproducibility of the statistical analyses.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI

issues.subcategory: Typographical and terminology errors affecting clarity
issues.description: Repeated errors such as 'Mechanical Amazon Turk', 'Solvic', 'asserts', 'Hypothese', and inconsistent terms like identifiable/identified victim reduce clarity and may indicate insufficient proofreading. While mostly minor, some terminology issues can obscure methodological details.
issues.quote: Mechanical Amazon Turk platform
